claim: Viral samples were collected at 41 time points spanning 8 months during the course of an influenza B infection in a severely immunocompromised host.
source: Viral samples were collected at 41 time points spanning 8 months during the course of an influenza B infection in a severely immunocompromised host (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of time points and duration of sample collection.

claim: After unsuccessful treatment with oseltamivir, zanamivir and nitazoxanide, a bone marrow transplant and favipiravir combination therapy led to the apparent clearance of infection.
source: After unsuccessful treatment with oseltamivir, zanamivir and nitazoxanide, a bone marrow transplant and favipiravir combination therapy led to the apparent clearance of infection.
evidence: The manuscript describes the treatment history and outcomes.

claim: Apart from a single exception, biweekly samples tested negative for influenza across a period of close to two months.
source: Apart from a single exception, biweekly samples tested negative for influenza across a period of close to two months.
evidence: The manuscript reports the testing results during a specific period.

claim: A subsequent resurgence of zanamivir-resistant infection was cleared by favipiravir and zanamivir in combination.
source: A subsequent resurgence of zanamivir-resistant infection was cleared by favipiravir and zanamivir in combination.
evidence: The manuscript describes the final treatment outcome.

claim: The mean viral load was close to the mean reported for a set of samples from hospitalised children with influenza.
source: The mean viral load (dashed horizontal line, red) was close to the mean reported for a set of samples from hospitalised children with influenza (dashed horizontal blue line) (Wishaupt et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript compares the viral load to published data and shows this in Figure 1A.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis of whole-genome viral consensus sequences showed the existence of non-trivial population structure, with at least two distinct clades emerging over time.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of whole-genome viral consensus sequences showed the existence of non-trivial population structure, with at least two distinct clades emerging over time (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1); we term these clades A and B.
evidence: The manuscript describes phylogenetic analysis results shown in figures.

claim: Having diverged, the two clades persisted across several months of infection.
source: Having diverged, the two clades persisted across several months of infection.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal persistence of the clades.

claim: Haplotype reconstruction showed that samples from clade B were comprised of distinct viral haplotypes to those from clade A.
source: Haplotype reconstruction showed that samples from clade B were comprised of distinct viral haplotypes to those from clade A; similar patterns were observed in different viral segments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes haplotype reconstruction results.

claim: From a common evolutionary origin, Clade B slowly evolved away from the initial consensus, while viruses in clade A stayed close in sequence space to this consensus.
source: We suggest that, from a common evolutionary origin, Clade B slowly evolved away from the initial consensus, while viruses in clade A stayed close in sequence space to this consensus.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the evolutionary patterns observed.

claim: The cladal structure suggests the existence of spatially distinct viral populations in the host, samples stochastically representing one population or the other.
source: The cladal structure suggests the existence of spatially distinct viral populations in the host, samples stochastically representing one population or the other.
evidence: The manuscript infers population structure from the observed cladal patterns.

claim: A method of linear regression was used to quantify the rate of viral evolution, measuring the genetic distance between samples as a function of increasing time between dates of sample collection.
source: A method of linear regression was used to quantify the rate of viral evolution, measuring the genetic distance between samples as a function of increasing time between dates of sample collection.
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical method used.

claim: The rate of viral evolution was inferred to be 0.051 substitutions per day (97.5% confidence interval 0.034 to 0.068).
source: We inferred a rate equivalent to 0.051 substitutions per day (97.5% confidence interval 0.034 to 0.068) (Figure 2A), equivalent to 7.94 substitutions genome-wide across 157 days of evolution.
evidence: The manuscript reports the calculated evolutionary rate with confidence intervals.

claim: The identified value of close to 40 substitutions is equivalent to a between-sample allele frequency difference of approximately +/- 0.3% per locus.
source: The identified value of close to 40 substitutions is equivalent to a between-sample allele frequency difference of approximately +/- 0.3% per locus.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the vertical intercept of the regression line.

claim: While considerable noise affects each sample, the dataset as a whole provides a clear signal of evolutionary change.
source: While considerable noise affects each sample, the dataset as a whole provides a clear signal of evolutionary change.
evidence: The manuscript assesses the quality of the evolutionary signal in the data.

claim: A simulation based analysis inferred an effective population size of 2.5 × 10^7 (95% confidence range 1.0 × 10^7 to 9.0 × 10^7) for viruses in clade A before the use of favipiravir.
source: A simulation based analysis, measuring the extent of evolution in idealised Wright-Fisher populations (Kimura and Crow, 1963), inferred an effective population size of 2.5 × 107 (95% confidence range 1.0 × 107 to 9.0 × 107) for viruses in clade A before the use of favipiravir (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the Ne estimate from Wright-Fisher simulations.

claim: This value is substantially larger than estimates made recently for within-host HIV infection.
source: This value is substantially larger than estimates made recently for within-host HIV infection (Pennings et al., 2014; Rouzine et al., 2014), and suggests that even weak selection could easily overcome genetic drift.
evidence: The manuscript compares the Ne estimate to published HIV estimates.

claim: Data from clade B gave a lower estimated value of 2 × 10^6, (95% confidence range 4 × 10^5 to 2 × 10^8).
source: Data from clade B gave a lower estimated value of 2 × 106, (95% confidence range 4 × 105 to 2 × 108) perhaps reflecting the less frequent observation of samples in that clade (Figure 2C,D), and the bottleneck induced by favipiravir, which was spanned by the data used in this calculation.
evidence: The manuscript reports the Ne estimate for clade B with explanation.

claim: The value of Ne is representative of the population after the initial establishment of infection; the initial expansion of the viral population was not represented in the data.
source: Our value of Ne is representative of the population after the initial establishment of infection; the initial expansion of the viral population was not represented in our data.
evidence: The manuscript clarifies the temporal scope of the Ne estimate.

claim: Population structure during the infection might have lowered the value obtained for Ne.
source: Population structure during the infection might have lowered the value we obtain (Whitlock and Barton, 1997).
evidence: The manuscript discusses potential biases in the Ne estimate.

claim: The partial onset of zanamivir resistant alleles is suggestive of sampling a random mixture of viruses from resistant and susceptible subpopulations.
source: The partial onset of zanamivir resistant alleles (Jackson et al., 2005), sporadically observed at intermediate frequency in clade A after the administration of the drug (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), is suggestive of sampling a random mixture of viruses from resistant and susceptible subpopulations.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the pattern of resistance alleles.

claim: The influence of positive selection might have led to an underestimate of Ne.
source: As such, the influence of positive selection might have led us to underestimate Ne.
evidence: The manuscript discusses potential biases in the method.

claim: Viral evolution was generally not driven by selection.
source: While viral evolution was generally not driven by selection (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), positive selection (e.g. for zanamivir resistance) would increase the rate of viral evolution, lowering our inferred value.
evidence: The manuscript assesses the role of selection in the observed evolution.

claim: Once an infection is established, selection will dominate the stochastic effects of drift upon within-host evolution.
source: Yet our result is clear. Once an infection is established, selection will dominate the stochastic effects of drift upon within-host evolution.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the Ne estimate.

claim: The dataset considered is particularly suited to the calculation due to the long period of infection combined with frequent sampling.
source: The dataset we considered is particularly suited to our calculation. The long period of infection combined with frequent sampling allowed for the characterisation of a slow rate of evolution amidst population structure and noise in the data.
evidence: The manuscript explains why the dataset is appropriate for the analysis.

claim: The absence of strong selection reduced the error in the inference approach, which assumed an idealised neutral population.
source: Further, the absence of strong selection reduced the error in our inference approach, which assumed an idealised neutral population.
evidence: The manuscript discusses the validity of the methodological assumptions.

claim: The approach was repeated on data describing long-term influenza A/H3N2 infection in four immunocompromised adults.
source: To provide further validation we repeated our approach on data describing long-term influenza A/H3N2 infection in four immunocompromised adults (Xue et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes validation using additional data.

claim: The estimates for Ne obtained from influenza A/H3N2 data were between 3 × 10^5 and 1 × 10^6.
source: The estimates for Ne we obtained, of between 3 × 105 and 1 × 106 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), while high, were smaller than for our flu B case, potentially being reduced by an increased influence of selection.
evidence: The manuscript reports Ne estimates from the validation analysis.

claim: The viral load in the influenza B case was high, representative of hospitalised cases of childhood influenza infection.
source: The viral load in the influenza B case was high, representative of hospitalised cases of childhood influenza infection.
evidence: The manuscript characterizes the viral load in the studied case.

claim: The magnitude of the inferred effective size, of order 10^7, suggests that selection will predominate over drift even in more typical cases.
source: However, the magnitude of our inferred effective size, of order 107, suggests that selection will predominate over drift even in more typical cases.
evidence: The manuscript extrapolates from the findings to typical cases.

claim: Mean CT values for influenza in non-hospitalised children have been reported as around 10 units lower than those for hospitalised cases.
source: Mean CT values for influenza in non-hospitalised children have been reported as around 10 units lower than those for hospitalised cases (Wishaupt et al., 2017); an order of magnitude calculation suggests an Ne, upon the establishment of infection, of approximately 104 in such cases.
evidence: The manuscript cites published data and performs a calculation.

claim: An order of magnitude calculation suggests an Ne, upon the establishment of infection, of approximately 10^4 in non-hospitalised cases.
source: Mean CT values for influenza in non-hospitalised children have been reported as around 10 units lower than those for hospitalised cases (Wishaupt et al., 2017); an order of magnitude calculation suggests an Ne, upon the establishment of infection, of approximately 104 in such cases.
evidence: The manuscript estimates Ne for non-hospitalised cases.

claim: The evolution of a measurable variant (i.e. at a frequency of 1% or above) will be dominated by selection of a magnitude of 1% or greater per generation.
source: It has the implication that the evolution of a measurable variant (i.e. at a frequency of 1% or above) will be dominated by selection of a magnitude of 1% or greater per generation (Rouzine et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript draws an implication from the Ne estimate.

claim: The result supports the idea that a tight transmission bottleneck followed by a short period of infection is sufficient to explain the observed lack of within-host variation in typical cases of influenza.
source: Our result supports the idea that a tight transmission bottleneck (McCrone et al., 2018; Valesano, 2020; Ghafari et al., 2020) followed by a short period of infection is sufficient to explain the observed lack of within-host variation in typical cases of influenza (Debbink et al., 2017; McCrone et al., 2018); the stochastic effects of genetic drift do not limit the impact of positive selection.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the findings in the context of published literature.

claim: The stochastic effects of genetic drift do not limit the impact of positive selection.
source: Our result supports the idea that a tight transmission bottleneck (McCrone et al., 2018; Valesano, 2020; Ghafari et al., 2020) followed by a short period of infection is sufficient to explain the observed lack of within-host variation in typical cases of influenza (Debbink et al., 2017; McCrone et al., 2018); the stochastic effects of genetic drift do not limit the impact of positive selection.
evidence: The manuscript states a conclusion about the relative importance of drift and selection.

claim: Variants arising through de novo mutation would require strong selection to reach a substantial frequency during infection.
source: Variants arising through de novo mutation would require strong selection to reach a substantial frequency during infection (Zhao et al., 2019), particularly if the onset of selection is delayed (Miao et al., 2010; Illingworth et al., 2014; Morris, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript discusses the requirements for de novo variants to increase in frequency.

claim: Selection does not usually have time to fix novel variants in the population, exceptions including the emergence of antiviral resistance and some cases of longer infection.
source: We suggest that, while not being confounded by drift, selection does not usually have time to fix novel variants in the population, exceptions including the emergence of antiviral resistance and some cases of longer infection (Xue et al., 2017; Gubareva et al., 1998; Snydman, 2006; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 2009; Imai et al., 2020; Rogers et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript proposes an explanation for the limited within-host adaptation.

claim: The result highlights the potential importance of longer infections in the adaptation of global influenza populations, particularly where some adaptive immune response remains.
source: Our result highlights the potential importance of longer infections in the adaptation of global influenza populations, particularly where some adaptive immune response remains.
evidence: The manuscript discusses implications for global influenza evolution.

claim: A newly emergent variant under strong positive selection increases faster than linearly in frequency.
source: A newly emergent variant under strong positive selection increases faster than linearly in frequency (Haldane, 1924).
evidence: The manuscript cites established population genetics theory.

claim: Given a large Ne, implying efficient selection, additional days of infection will have a disproportionate influence upon the potential transmission of adaptive variants.
source: Given a large Ne, implying efficient selection, additional days of infection will have a disproportionate influence upon the potential transmission of adaptive variants.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the Ne estimate and selection theory.

claim: Longer infections may be an important area of study in the quest to better understand global influenza virus evolution.
source: However, our work suggests that longer-term infections may be an important area of study in the quest to better understand global influenza virus evolution.
evidence: The manuscript suggests a research direction based on the findings.

claim: Strains of the influenza virus form coherent global populations, yet exist at the level of single infections in individual hosts.
source: Strains of the influenza virus form coherent global populations, yet exist at the level of single infections in individual hosts.
evidence: The abstract states this as a fundamental characteristic of influenza.

claim: The effective population size for influenza infection was estimated to be Ne of 2.5 × 10^7 (95% confidence range 1.0 × 10^7 to 9.0 × 10^7).
source: Examining whole-genome sequence data describing a chronic case of influenza B in a severely immunocompromised child we infer an Ne of 2.5 × 107 (95% confidence range 1.0 × 107 to 9.0 × 107) suggesting that genetic drift is of minimal importance during an established influenza infection.
evidence: The abstract reports the main finding of the study.

claim: Genetic drift is of minimal importance during an established influenza infection.
source: Examining whole-genome sequence data describing a chronic case of influenza B in a severely immunocompromised child we infer an Ne of 2.5 × 107 (95% confidence range 1.0 × 107 to 9.0 × 107) suggesting that genetic drift is of minimal importance during an established influenza infection.
evidence: The abstract states this as an inference from the Ne estimate.

claim: Positive selection during within-host infection is primarily limited by the typically short period of infection.
source: Our result, supported by data from influenza A infection, suggests that positive selection during within-host infection is primarily limited by the typically short period of infection.
evidence: The abstract states this as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Atypically long infections may have a disproportionate influence upon global patterns of viral evolution.
source: Atypically long infections may have a disproportionate influence upon global patterns of viral evolution.
evidence: The abstract states this as an implication of the findings.

claim: On a global level, influenza populations exhibit coherent behaviour.
source: On a global level, populations exhibit coherent behaviour (Buonagurio et al., 1986; Fitch et al., 1997; Bedford et al., 2015), evolving rapidly under collective host immune pressure (Ferguson et al., 2003; Grenfell et al., 2004).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature on global influenza evolution.

claim: Influenza populations evolve rapidly under collective host immune pressure.
source: On a global level, populations exhibit coherent behaviour (Buonagurio et al., 1986; Fitch et al., 1997; Bedford et al., 2015), evolving rapidly under collective host immune pressure (Ferguson et al., 2003; Grenfell et al., 2004).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature on immune-driven evolution.

claim: Recent studies of within-host infection have suggested that positive selection does not strongly influence evolution at this smaller scale.
source: Despite the clear role for selection in global influenza populations, recent studies of within-host infection have suggested that positive selection does not strongly influence evolution at this smaller scale (Debbink et al., 2017; McCrone et al., 2018; Han et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites recent literature on within-host selection.

claim: Contrasting explanations have been given for the limited role of positive selection within-host, with suggestions either that selection is intrinsically inefficient, being dominated by stochastic processes, or that while selection is efficient, a mismatch in timing between the peak viral titre and the host adaptive immune response prevents selection from taking effect.
source: Contrasting explanations have been given for this, with suggestions either that selection at the within-host level is intrinsically inefficient, being dominated by stochastic processes (McCrone et al., 2018), or that while selection is efficient, a mismatch in timing between the peak viral titre and the host adaptive immune response prevents selection from taking effect (Han et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction summarizes competing hypotheses from the literature.

claim: The balance between selection and genetic drift is determined by the effective size of the population, denoted Ne.
source: The balance between these factors is determined by the effective size of the population, denoted Ne.
evidence: The introduction states a fundamental principle of population genetics.

claim: If Ne is high, selection will outweigh genetic drift, even where differences in viral fitness are small.
source: If Ne is high, selection will outweigh genetic drift, even where differences in viral fitness are small (Rouzine et al., 2001).
evidence: The introduction cites a theoretical result about Ne and selection.

claim: If Ne is low, less fit viruses are more likely to outcompete their fitter compatriots.
source: By contrast, if Ne is low, less fit viruses are more likely to outcompete their fitter compatriots.
evidence: The introduction states a consequence of low Ne.

claim: Estimating Ne is a difficult task, with a long history of method development in this area.
source: Estimating Ne is a difficult task, with a long history of method development in this area (Wright, 1938; Wang et al., 2016; Khatri and Burt, 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites historical and recent literature on Ne estimation methods.

claim: A simple measure of Ne may be calculated by matching the genetic change in allele frequencies in a population with the changes occurring in an idealised population evolving under genetic drift.
source: A simple measure of Ne may be calculated by matching the genetic change in allele frequencies in a population with the changes occurring in an idealised population evolving under genetic drift (Kimura and Crow, 1963).
evidence: The introduction describes a classical method for estimating Ne.

claim: Such estimates are vulnerable to distortion, for example being reduced by the effect of positive selection in a population.
source: However, such estimates are vulnerable to distortion, for example being reduced by the effect of positive selection in a population.
evidence: The introduction discusses limitations of simple Ne estimation methods.

claim: Where the global influenza A/H3N2 population is driven by repeated selective sweeps, a neutral estimation method suggests a value for Ne not much greater than 100.
source: Where the global influenza A/H3N2 population is driven by repeated selective sweeps (Fitch et al., 1991; Rambaut et al., 2008; Strelkowa and Lässig, 2012) a neutral estimation method suggests a value for Ne not much greater than 100 (Bedford et al., 2010).
evidence: The introduction cites published estimates of Ne for global influenza.

claim: Methods for jointly estimating Ne and selection exist, but they are limited in considering only a few loci in linkage disequilibrium.
source: While methods for jointly estimating Ne and selection exist, they are limited in considering only a few loci in linkage disequililbrium (Bollback et al., 2008; Feder et al., 2014; Foll et al., 2014; Terhorst et al., 2015; Rousseau et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction discusses limitations of more sophisticated Ne estimation methods.

claim: Non-trivial population structure can affect estimates of Ne.
source: Non-trivial population structure can affect estimates (Laporte and Charlesworth, 2002); a growing body of evidence supports the existence of structure in within-host influenza infection (Lakdawala et al., 2015; Sobel Leonard et al., 2017a; Richard et al., 2018; Hamada et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on population structure effects on Ne estimation.

claim: A growing body of evidence supports the existence of structure in within-host influenza infection.
source: Non-trivial population structure can affect estimates (Laporte and Charlesworth, 2002); a growing body of evidence supports the existence of structure in within-host influenza infection (Lakdawala et al., 2015; Sobel Leonard et al., 2017a; Richard et al., 2018; Hamada et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on within-host population structure.

claim: Noise from sequencing and unrepresentative sample collection combine, potentially confounding estimates of Ne in viral populations.
source: While careful experimental techniques can reduce sequencing error (McCrone and Lauring, 2016), noise from sequencing and unrepresentative sample collection combine (Illingworth et al., 2017), potentially confounding estimates of Ne in viral populations (Lumby et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction discusses sources of error in Ne estimation.

claim: If Ne is high, any signal of drift can be obscured by noise.
source: If Ne is high, any signal of drift can be obscured by noise.
evidence: The introduction discusses a challenge in estimating high Ne values.

claim: An absence of cell-mediated immunity led to the persistence of the infection for several months.
source: While the viral load of the infection was not unusual for a hospitalised childhood infection (Wishaupt et al., 2017), an absence of cell-mediated immunity led to the persistence of the infection for several months (Lumby et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction describes the clinical characteristics of the case.

claim: The reduced role of positive selection, combined with novel methods to account for noise and population structure, enabled an improved inference of Ne.
source: Given extensive sequence data collected during infection, the reduced role of positive selection, combined with novel methods to account for noise and population structure, enabled an improved inference of Ne.
evidence: The introduction explains why the dataset is suitable for Ne estimation.

claim: The large effective size inferred suggests that selection acts in an efficient manner during an established influenza infection.
source: The large effective size we infer suggests that selection acts in an efficient manner during an established influenza infection.
evidence: The introduction states a key conclusion of the study.

claim: Even in more typical cases, the influence of positive selection is likely to be limited only by the duration of infection.
source: Even in more typical cases, the influence of positive selection is likely to be limited only by the duration of infection.
evidence: The introduction states an implication of the findings for typical infections.

claim: Clinical details of the case, and the use of viral sequence data in evaluating the effectiveness of clinical intervention, have been described elsewhere.
source: Clinical details of the case, and the use of viral sequence data in evaluating the effectiveness of clinical intervention, have been described elsewhere (Lumby et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript references a previous publication for clinical details.

claim: The rate of evolution in both clades was slower at non-synonymous sites than at synonymous sites, suggesting a general pattern of purifying selection at non-synonymous sites.
source: The rate of evolution in both clades was slower at non-synonymous sites than at synonymous sites, suggesting a general pattern of purifying selection at non-synonymous sites.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2 caption states this finding.

claim: Change in the population was not as a whole driven by positive selection.
source: Change in the population was not as a whole driven by positive selection.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2 caption states this conclusion.

claim: The consensus glutamate nucleotide was sometimes replaced by glycine, valine, and alanine.
source: The consensus glutamate nucleotide (blue) was sometimes replaced by glycine (green), valine (yellow), and alanine (red).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 caption describes the observed substitutions.

claim: Glycine and alanine are associated with zanamivir resistance in influenza B.
source: Glycine and alanine are associated with zanamivir resistance in influenza B.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 caption states this association.

claim: Variants at higher frequencies were identified at more consistent frequencies than variants at lower frequencies.
source: Variants at higher frequencies were identified at more consistent frequencies than variants at lower frequencies.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 5 caption describes the pattern in replicate data.

claim: High frequency variants were very reliably identified, but the reliability of identifying variants was significantly impaired at lower frequencies.
source: While high frequency variants were very reliably identified, the reliability of identifying variants was significantly impaired at lower frequencies.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 7 caption describes the frequency-dependent reliability.

claim: Samples in the dataset were split following RNA extraction with replicate sets of RNA being processed and sequenced independently.
source: Samples in this dataset were split following RNA extraction with replicate sets of RNA being processed and sequenced independently.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 5 caption describes the experimental design.

claim: The distribution of minor allele frequencies across the genome was reasonably constant between samples for which a good read depth was achieved.
source: Regarding these allele frequencies we note that the distribution of minor allele frequencies across the genome was reasonably constant between samples for which a good read depth was achieved (Figure 2—figure supplement 4; read depths for these data have previously been reported Lumby et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript describes the consistency of allele frequency distributions.

claim: Rates of evolution calculated from the sequence data were rates of change per day whereas a Wright-Fisher simulation gives an estimated rate of evolution per generation.
source: Rates of evolution calculated from the sequence data were rates of change per day whereas a Wright-Fisher simulation gives an estimated rate of evolution per generation.
evidence: The manuscript explains the need for scaling between time units.

claim: The experimentally ascertained estimate of generation time for influenza B is 10 hours per generation.
source: We therefore scaled the former to match the experimentally ascertained estimate of 10 hr per generation for influenza B (Nobusawa and Sato, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published estimate of influenza B generation time.

claim: Intra-segment recombination was assumed to be negligible.
source: Intra-segment recombination was assumed to be negligible (Boni et al., 2008), while reassortment between segments was neglected in line with evidence from cases of human infection (Sobel Leonard et al., 2017a).
evidence: The manuscript states assumptions of the simulation model.

claim: Reassortment between segments was neglected in line with evidence from cases of human infection.
source: Intra-segment recombination was assumed to be negligible (Boni et al., 2008), while reassortment between segments was neglected in line with evidence from cases of human infection (Sobel Leonard et al., 2017a).
evidence: The manuscript states assumptions of the simulation model.

claim: The experimental pipeline used has been shown to perform well in capturing within-host viral diversity.
source: While the experimental pipeline we used has been shown to perform well in capturing within-host viral diversity (STOP-HCV Consortium et al., 2016), the possibility remains that sequencing could contribute additional diversity to the initial populations used in our simulation.
evidence: The manuscript cites validation of the sequencing pipeline.

claim: Data from a previous study describing the repeat sequencing of hepatitis C virus (HCV) samples from a host were used to estimate the extent to which the sequencing process led to the false identification of variants.
source: To achieve this, we used data from a previous study describing the repeat sequencing of hepatitis C virus (HCV) samples from a host (Illingworth et al., 2017); data in this previous study were collected using the same sequencing pipeline as that used to collect the data considered here and therefore provide a generic measure of the level of false positive variation.
evidence: The manuscript describes the use of HCV data to estimate false positive rates.

claim: The HCV data were collected using the same sequencing pipeline as that used to collect the influenza data.
source: To achieve this, we used data from a previous study describing the repeat sequencing of hepatitis C virus (HCV) samples from a host (Illingworth et al., 2017); data in this previous study were collected using the same sequencing pipeline as that used to collect the data considered here and therefore provide a generic measure of the level of false positive variation.
evidence: The manuscript justifies the use of HCV data for estimating error rates.

claim: The data analyzed, coded as HCV01 in the original study, comprised four clinical HCV samples, each of which was split following nucleic acid extraction.
source: The data we analysed, coded as HCV01 in the original study, comprised four clinical HCV samples, each of which was split following nucleic acid extraction.
evidence: The manuscript describes the HCV dataset used.

claim: DNase depletion led to samples with lower read depth.
source: Some replicate samples were processed using a DNase depletion method before all samples went through cDNA synthesis, library preparation and sequencing. DNase depletion led to samples with lower read depth; we here compared sequence data collected from the non-depleted replicates of each sample.
evidence: The manuscript describes the effect of DNase depletion on sequencing.

claim: Only 56 sites, fewer than 0.1% of the more than 73 thousand sites sequenced, had more than one minority variant at a frequency greater than 1%.
source: We note that, of the more than 73 thousand sites sequenced, only 56, fewer than 0.1%, had more than one minority variant at a frequency greater than 1%.
evidence: The manuscript reports the frequency of multi-allelic sites.

claim: The assumption was made that the false negative rate of detecting variants is equal to zero.
source: We begin by assuming that the false negative rate of detecting variants is equal to zero. That is, where we do not see a variant in the sequence data, we assume that a variant is never actually present.
evidence: The manuscript states an assumption of the false positive rate estimation.

claim: This is a conservative step in so far as unobserved variation is never added to the population.
source: This is a conservative step in so far as we never add unobserved variation to the population.
evidence: The manuscript justifies the assumption as conservative.

claim: To account for the neglect of mutation, a frequency cutoff was applied to the simulation data.
source: To account for our neglect of mutation, a frequency cutoff was applied to our simulation data.
evidence: The manuscript describes a correction applied to the simulations.

claim: Under a pure process of genetic drift, low-frequency variants in the population are likely to die out, reaching a frequency of zero.
source: Under a pure process of genetic drift, low-frequency variants in our population are likely to die out, reaching a frequency of zero.
evidence: The manuscript states an expected outcome of genetic drift.

claim: In a real population, variants would not reach zero frequency, being sustained at low frequencies by a balance of mutation and purifying selection.
source: In a real population, this would not occur, variants being sustained at low frequencies by a balance of mutation and purifying selection (Haldane, 1937; Haigh, 1978).
evidence: The manuscript cites theory on mutation-selection balance.

claim: A minimum minority allele frequency of 0.1% was imposed on the simulation data.
source: To correct for this we post-processed the initial and final frequency values from our simulations before calculating our distance, imposing a minimum minority allele frequency of 0.1%.
evidence: The manuscript describes the frequency cutoff applied.

claim: The choice of 0.1% threshold is conservative, leading to a conservatively low estimate of Ne.
source: The choice of threshold here is conservative; leading to a conservatively low estimate of Ne.
evidence: The manuscript assesses the impact of the threshold choice.

claim: Confidence intervals for the effective population size were calculated as the overlap of 97.5% confidence intervals for the evolutionary rates in the observed data and estimated from the simulated statistics.
source: Confidence intervals for the effective population size were calculated as the overlap of 97.5% confidence intervals for the evolutionary rates in the observed data, calculated from the regression for the real data, and estimated from the simulated statistics.
evidence: The manuscript describes the method for calculating confidence intervals.

claim: The overlap of confidence intervals gives an approximate 95% confidence interval for Ne.
source: The overlap of these values gives an approximate 95% confidence interval for Ne.
evidence: The manuscript explains the interpretation of the confidence interval calculation.

claim: Data describing the evolution of the infection was generated as part of a previous study.
source: Sequence data describing the evolution of the infection was generated as part of a previous study (Lumby et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript references the source of the sequence data.

claim: Data, edited to remove human genome sequence data, have been deposited in the Sequence Read Archive with BioProject ID PRJNA601176.
source: Data, edited to remove human genome sequence data, have been deposited in the Sequence Read Archive with BioProject ID PRJNA601176.
evidence: The manuscript provides data availability information.

claim: The HCV data used in validating the sequencing pipeline were previously deposited in the Sequence Read Archive with BioProject ID PRJNA380188.
